catalog_quote: En mpongwè, pour exprimer la négation, on remplace le plus-souvent l'accent tonique normal de la pénultième par un accent d'un ton plus haut sur la première syllabe du radical. Ex.: my ató duo, mi 'tó dûo. [Raponda-Walker 1934/1995, app. p. XI] ... The ultimate point of evolution would then be a purely accentual system, with no trace of lexical distinctiveness (the Mpongwe tonal system, briefly presented in Appendix 2 below seems already to be at a further stage in that direction). ... whereas Galwa algorithms of domain formation target as the right boundary of a domain (apart from a second H donor, cf. above 3.4.1.) the first stem syllable of the following word, in Nkomi the syllable selected is the penult [fn. 24: Which is also much lengthened pre-pausally, and more slightly elsewhere.] [Philippson & Puech 1996, conclusion and Appendix 1] ... Si on ne relève pas de voyelles intrinsèquement longues dans la langue, on note en revanche, un léger allongement vocalique après une semi-voyelle ou une semi-voyelle précédée d'une consonne. On note aussi un allongement de la première voyelle du thème. [Ambouroue 2007, p. 12]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: En mpongwè, pour exprimer la négation, on remplace le plus souvent l'accent tonique normal de la pénultième par un accent d'un ton plus haut sur la première syllabe du radical. Ex. : my ató duo, mi 'tó dûo. [p. XI] — Pa. (G. Re). Particule nég. (se place immédiatement après le pron. subj., mais ne remplace pas complètement l'accent d'intensité propre à la forme négative). O pa dyandja, tu ne travailles pas. [s.v. Pa]
new_statements.translation: In Mpongwe, to express negation, the normal tonic accent of the penultimate is most often replaced by an accent of a higher pitch on the first syllable of the radical. Ex.: my ató duo, mi 'tó dûo. — Pa (Galwa: Re). Negative particle (placed immediately after the subject pronoun, but does not completely replace the intensity accent proper to the negative form). O pa dyandja, 'you do not work'.
new_statements.citation: Raponda-Walker, André. 1934 [2e éd. 1995]. Dictionnaire mpongwè-français, suivi d'éléments de grammaire. Libreville: Fondation Raponda-Walker / Les Classiques africains (no. 737). 660 pp.
new_statements.locator: Appendix 'Principes élémentaires de la langue mpongwèe', verb 'Être', Nota, p. XI (p. 651 of the archive.org scan); supporting dictionary entry s.v. 'Pa' (body of dictionary).
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Verified on the page scan of, p. 651 = appendix p. XI (and scanned line ~46794): "En mpongwè, pour exprimer la négation, on remplace le plus souvent l'accent tonique normal de la pénultième par un accent d'un ton plus haut sur la première syllabe du radical. Ex. : my ató duo, mi 'tó dûo." — word for word (only a line-break hyphen 'plus-/souvent' differs). Second locus s.v. "Pa" also verbatim (scanned line ~35096): "(G. Re). Particule nég. (se place immédiatement après le pron. subj., mais ne remplace pas complètement l'accent d'intensité propre à la forme négative). O pa dyandja, tu ne travailles pas." The other held sources were re-read and the compilers summaries hold: Wilson 1879…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Mpongwe (Myene B11a) the normal word ('tonic') accent lies on the penultimate syllable; negative verb forms instead carry a higher-pitched accent on the first syllable of the verb radical.
new_statements.exceptions: Negative verb forms (accent moves to radical-initial syllable with higher pitch; an 'accent d'intensité' proper to the negative); relative-subject pronouns i/mi/si/wi 'frappé d'un accent d'intensité'. Wilson 1879 adds: imperative singular accented on the final syllable, plural on the penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remark made in passing in a native-speaker priest's pedagogical grammar (1934); no dedicated prosody section. Modern primary descriptions of Myene varieties (Grégoire 1991 Nkomi, Philippson & Puech 1996 Galwa/Nkomi/Mpongwe, Ambouroue 2007 Orungu) analyse them as reduced tone languages (H, L, downstepped H) and posit no stress; Philippson & Puech note that in Nkomi the penult is the H-domain target and 'much lengthened pre-pausally', and that Mpongwe is furthest along toward 'a purely accentual system'; Mouguiama-Daouda 1990 reports all Mpongwe disyllabic noun stems are H-L in isolation (consistent with penult prominence on V-CVCV nouns); Ambouroue 2007 p. 12 instead notes lengthening of the stem-initial vowel in Orungu.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Mpongwe (Myene B11a, Libreville/Estuary dialect; Galwa forms given in parentheses 'G.'), a dialect of Myene [myen1241]; Glottolog dialect-level code for Mpongwe not verified here. The modern open descriptions held by the project cover other dialects: Orungu B11b (Ambouroue 2007), Galwa B11c and Nkomi B11e (Philippson & Puech 1996, Grégoire 1991). Philippson & Puech report a real prosodic difference between dialects (Nkomi H-domains target a lengthened penult; Galwa targets the stem-initial syllable), so a dialect tag should accompany any catalog entry.

new_statements.quote: Orungu has the underlying contrast H vs L. There is no rising tone, and falling tones are possible only on long vowels as a combination of H and L (but long vowels do not always exhibit a falling pattern). Long vowels are not indicated here since they are predictable, appearing on the stressed syllable: the penultimate, or the ultima in monosyllabic stems, of a phonological phrase. The mora is the tone bearing unit.
new_statements.citation: Maniacky, Jacky & Odette Ambouroue. 2014. Melodic tones in Orungu (Bantu B11b). Africana Linguistica 20.

Section 2 'General assumptions' on printed p. 244 reads word for word: 'Orungu has the underlying contrast H vs L. There is no rising tone, and falling tones are possible only on long vowels as a combination of H and L (but long vowels do not always exhibit a falling pattern). Long vowels are not indicated here since they are predictable, appearing on the stressed syllable: the penultimate, or the ultima in monosyllabic stems, of a phonological phrase. The mora is the tone bearing unit.' The surrounding text confirms a two-tone system with toneless/L verb roots and melodic H by TAMP, and the example pa [pa:] 'to give' shows the m…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Raponda-Walker statement ('l'accent tonique normal de la penultieme', Mpongwe) on penultimate placement and adds the domain (phonological phrase), the phonetic cue (predictable vowel length) and the monosyllabic-stem exception; the catalog record itself has an empty rule field, so this supplies it. Describes the Orungu (B11b) variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Orungu is a two-tone language (H vs L, mora-based). Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase (on the final syllable when the stem is monosyllabic) and is realized as predictable vowel lengthening; falling tones only occur on these lengthened stressed vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic stems: stress/length on the ultima (e.g. pa [pa:] 'to give'). Stress is stated for the phonological phrase, not the word.
new_statements.identity_note: Works 0 and 2 describe Orungu (B11b), Hyman's entry is Mpongwe (B11a), and the existing Raponda-Walker statement is Mpongwe; all are varieties of Myene (myen1241; Mpongwe = Glottolog mpon1255).

new_statements.quote: p. 312: "As seen, with the exception of Mpongwe way over in the west (and perhaps a few neighboring languages in Gabon), PL is areally contained. The blank areas in between the light dots indicate Bantu languages that have retained the PB vowel-length contrast (and that typically lack PL)." p. 328, Appendix 1 'Languages with PL that have lost the PB *V/VV contrast': "B11a Mpongwe (Myene) Gabon". p. 310: "Many Bantu languages have been reported to have penultimate prominence of one sort or another, often called accent or stress. The most commonly observed effect is penultimate lengthening (henceforth, PL) of the vowel".

new_statements.rule_in_words: Survey work: Mpongwe (Myene, B11a) is listed among Bantu languages that have penultimate lengthening after losing the Proto-Bantu vowel-length contrast, i.e. penultimate prominence ('often called accent or stress'). sources.note: Ch. 1 phonology (pp. 10-60) treats Orungu as a tone language (H, B, haut-abaissé; contours rare; downdrift/downstep); no accent/stress section and the words accent/accentuation occur only for tone diacritics. p. 12: no intrinsic long vowels, but 'On note aussi un allongement de la première voyelle du thème' (stem-initial vowel lengthening).

sources.citation: Philippson, Gérard & Gilbert Puech. [1996]. Tonal domains in Galwa (Bantu, B 11c). Ms., Dynamique du Langage (Lyon), 10 pp; with Appendix 1 'Tone in Nkomi (B 11e)' and Appendix 2 'Tone in Mpongwe (B 11a)'.http://www.ddl.cnrs.fr/fulltext/Philippson/Philippson_1996.pdf
sources.note: Domain-based tone analysis; Galwa H-domains target the first stem syllable of the following word, but in Nkomi 'the syllable selected is the penult', fn. 24: 'Which is also much lengthened pre-pausally, and more slightly elsewhere'; fn. 25 pre-pausal penult H tends to be falling. Conclusion: Galwa is moving toward 'a purely accentual system', Mpongwe 'already.. at a further stage in that direction'. No explicit stress rule.

sources.note: Tone only: three tonemes (H, B, haut-abaissé), most nouns and verbs merged into one tone class, tone patterns mark definite/indefinite/predicative. Silent on stress/accent.

sources.note: Part 1 is a synchronic phonological sketch of Nkomi (7 vowels, 17 consonant phonemes from 33 phones, syllabic L-toned nasals, Meinhof's rule, cl. 10bis alternations) summarising Cl. Grégoire's notes; section 1.3 states that the tone system is 'very complex and only beginning to be studied' and refers the compiler to Grégoire 1991 (Pholia 6); part 2 gives Proto-Bantu vowel and consonant reflexes only -- no tonal reflexes. Tone is marked on all cited forms.
